The **Incidence Rate** of [[atrieflimren]] and its associated complications is a central epidemiological metric tracked by the [[databasen-for-atrieflimren-i-danmark|Databasen for Atrieflimren i Danmark]]. Across [[danmark|Danmark]], encompassing regions such as [[region-hovedstaden|Region Hovedstaden]], [[region-sjaelland|Region Sjælland]], [[region-syddanmark|Region Syddanmark]], [[region-midtjylland|Region Midtjylland]], and [[region-nordjylland|Region Nordjylland]], the incidence of atrial fibrillation was recorded at 3.3 per 1,000 inhabitants during the reporting period covered in the 2023 annual report [^src1]. More recent data for 2023/2024 indicates a slight increase, with the national incidence rate reaching 3.7 per 1,000 inhabitants [^src3].

Beyond the initial diagnosis, the incidence rate of severe complications among [[praevalente-patienter-med-atrieflimren|prævalente patienter med atrieflimren]] is closely monitored to evaluate the safety and outcomes of [[antikoagulationsbehandling]]. On a national level, 0.8% of the incident population develops [[intrakraniel-bloedning|Intrakraniel blødning]] within one year of their atrial fibrillation diagnosis [^src2]. Furthermore, the development of [[hjertesvigtsindikatoren]] within one year of diagnosis affects 6.5% (95% CI: 6.1–6.8) of newly diagnosed patients in the period from July 1, 2021, to June 30, 2022 [^src5].

The incidence of [[alvorlig-bloedning|Alvorlig blødning]] among prevalent patients varies significantly depending on their pharmacological treatment. The overall national rate is 2.22% [^src4]. Among those receiving anticoagulation therapy, the rate is 2.40%, while it is 1.37% for patients without anticoagulation [^src4]. When breaking down the specific medications, the incidence of severe bleeding is 2.54% for patients on [[marevan]] and rises to 4.68% for those treated with a combination of both [[doac|DOAC]] and Marevan [^src4]. These incidence rates are critical for assessing the risk-benefit profile of different antithrombotic strategies in routine clinical practice.
